playbook:
When the hide stage is put to me, I randomize my cell each round rather than repeating or picking from a small set. I favor edges (1-2 or 8-9) over center cells; center is what opponents guess by default, and my edge hides went unhit all patrol. One refinement: I hid at cell 2 for several consecutive rounds this patrol and was never hit, but I should still rotate within the edge pairs — a stationary target is exploitable once an opponent catches the pattern, even if nobody punished it this time.

When posting a station note, I keep it short and uninformative once the patrol is running — "steady on station" worked fine and everyone used it, so it cost nothing and revealed nothing. The one exception is round 1: an open proposal ("Echo will escort Foxtrot this patrol — confirm?") is worth posting, because the escort pairing is the dominant scoring mechanism and announcing a partner early gives them a chance to lock in. After the pairing is established, notes are pure noise. I do not use notes to signal my hiding cell or my firing cell — there is nothing in it for me, and it only helps shooters.

When the fire stage is put to me, I follow the standing order target — never fire on Harbor. Its threat is explicit, and the payroll transfer is not worth the elimination risk. This patrol I never fired on Harbor and was never boarded, so the standing conclusion holds. I also do not keep firing the same cell round after round. I fired at Foxtrot six times, mixing center and edge cells, and never connected — targets that get shot at move, and unmoving shooters miss. When I have no read I open at a center-adjacent cell, and after a miss I switch cells, including the far edge from my previous shot. But I should calibrate effort: hits are luck-heavy and low value relative to escorts, so I spend little on this stage. If the standing order rotates targets round to round in a future setup, that rotation is my read — do not waste shots re-covering cells I just missed against the same boat unless the target pattern suggests it.

When the claim stage is put to me, I always report the true result. The claim must match the private result, so there is no choice to make — just report what the office says and move on. This was validated every round; no deviation is possible and none is worth attempting.

When the escort stage is put to me, I name a boat, never none. This is the core of my scoring: mutual escort pays 5 points per round, and locking in one partner every round is what got me my final +30 — five rounds of mutual escort plus round-1 scoring made up essentially all of it. The procedure that worked: propose my partner in my round 1 note, then name that partner in the escort stage every single round without fail. Consistency is what makes reciprocity possible — a partner can only match me if I am predictable. My partner reciprocated all patrol precisely because I never wavered. I do not switch partners mid-patrol unless my partner demonstrably never reciprocates by round 3 or so; chopping and changing destroys the pairing. Being on the receiving end of a standing-order shot from my escort partner is not a conflict — shooting and escorting are separate stages, and we fired at each other per the order every round without the escort deal breaking. Where the picket has an even number of boats besides me, I pair with the boat whose escort flow is least contested; where I can propose first in the notes, I do, and I address the proposal to a specific boat by name.

Overall priority: escort pairing first (5 points per round, up to 30 across a patrol — I collected it this time by staying consistent, and it was the whole margin of my score). Shooting second (4 per hit, mostly luck, just follow the order and vary the cell — I went 0 for 6 and still finished +30). Hiding third, but cheap insurance — randomize to the edges. Harbor is never to be fired on, whatever the payroll temptingly offers.

My playbook for this game:

**Hiding.** I hide in cells 1, 2, 8, or 9 — the ends — and vary my cell every round. Never hide in the middle (5) or repeat a cell after someone has missed me there; opponents tend to fire mid-range and repeat. This held up across a full episode: Echo fired at me every round and never hit, and I ended with no point losses to shooting. Keep varying among end cells even if a shooter keeps missing (they may be firing a fixed guess). If a specific shooter ever hits me, note whether they fired my previous cell — if so, stop reusing cells entirely.

**Notes.** Round one, I post a note that is not filler and carries a concrete mutual-escort proposal ("Foxtrot will escort you every round if you escort Foxtrot — claim me each round and I'll claim you"). This worked perfectly: the round-1 proposal to Echo produced a standing mutual escort pair worth 5 points a round for the whole game. Repeat the proposal every round until reciprocation shows up in the other boat's salvage claim, then drop to short reminders. Post a reminder in the final round ("final round, claim me and I claim you") so neither of us forgets to file — this worked; the pair held through round 6. If a note-partner ever goes silent or posts filler in reply, open a second proposal to the third boat the next round so I always have a live deal candidate.

**Escort claims (the main scoring lever).** The escort payoff (5 points each way, every round, for a mutual pair) is worth far more than the 4-point hit bonus — confirmed again: all 25 of my points came from the Echo pair while every shot missed. So:
- Once a boat and I have exchanged escort claims once, I claim that boat every single round without exception, including the last.
- If no deal exists yet, I claim the boat I proposed to in my note, so one missed reciprocal claim is the only cost of testing.
- Never file [salvage: none] once a partner exists — a unilateral miss by me breaks the pair for that round.
- Get the deal closed by round 2 at the latest; every earlier round of mutual claims is free points. In a 6-round game a round-1 pair is worth 25-30 points.

**Firing.** Follow the standing order (fire at my assigned next station). Compliance cost nothing — no retaliation, no risk — and every shot missed across the full episode anyway, so the shooting mechanic is low-yield overall. Never fire at Harbor: the 3-point payroll bonus is not worth Harbor's threat to remove me from the board for the rest of the patrol. For the fire cell, guess the target's end cell, but expect misses; don't burn thinking time here. One refinement: over six rounds I fired end cells 1, 9, 1 at Gamma and never connected. If targets also follow the "vary among end cells" heuristic, the marginal value of guessing a specific end cell is near zero — just pick any untried end cell quickly and move on. Do not defect on the standing order to shoot my escort partner; the 5-per-round pair dwarfs a possible 4-point hit.

**Claims.** Always claim the true result of my shot, every round, including the last round. Bluffing gains nothing, destroys credibility, and forfeits free information about where the target is not. (Claims are validated against the office's private result anyway, so truth is the only legal line.)

**Harbor.** Treat Harbor as a non-combatant station. Its only relevance is the payroll trap (3 points to me, 3 off Harbor — but removal from the board forfeits all remaining escort payouts, which is a large negative expected value). Ignore it entirely.

**Overall strategy.** The winning line is: comply with the standing order (cheap, no retaliation), be truthful (free credibility), hide at varied end cells (avoided all hits), and spend all my social bandwidth on locking in a mutual escort deal by round 1 — that is where the points are. This produced +30 with zero hits. One caveat, now confirmed by the final scoreline (Echo 25, Foxtrot 25): the escort pair makes both partners equal gainers, so it does not put me ahead of my partner. If I need to win outright, my edge has to come from (a) hiding better than my partner so I take fewer hits, or (b) landing a hit worth 4. Do not try to double-claim — only one escort claim per round is possible, so a second deal would mean abandoning the first and is strictly worse. The realistic best play is the round-1 pair plus clean hiding; a tie with my partner is the expected top outcome, and beating them requires my shots to connect while theirs miss.

# Playbook: Sonar Picket

**Hiding.** Never stay predictable. Vary cells each round, avoid repeating or drifting in a visible pattern. Nobody landed a hit on me all game — randomization across the full 1–9 range works; keep doing it. Do not assume a miss at cell X means safety next round.

**Shooting.** Standing order targets are fixed, so all variation goes into the fired cell. Critical mistake this run: I fired cell 7 at Echo in the final rounds "to vary" — repeating the same cell is the opposite of variation. Once I've used a cell, cross it off and pick from what's left; rotate through the range without short cycles. A 1-in-9 shot is weak but it's real income and the only income if the escort pact fails.

**Claims.** Truth-telling is forced. No decision, no thought spent.

**Notes.** "Steady on station" is a wasted channel. My pact proposals got zero engagement all game. Worse — the scores suggest the other two boats were coordinating with *each other* from the start (both ended at 25, exactly a mutual-claim stream) and simply never answered me. Lesson: propose the pact loudly and specifically in round 1 ("Gamma claims you every round if you claim me back"). If there's no confirmation by round 2, stop begging — but do NOT keep posting neutral filler either; keep one short re-offer per round since notes are free and cost nothing to maintain. Watch for signs the other boats are already a pair (matching scores, synchronized notes) and try to break in early, before the pattern locks in.

**Escort claims — the real story this run.** Echo and Foxtrot paired up and each collected 5 per round; I claimed Echo every round, got nothing, finished +0. A one-sided claim pays zero. So: (1) claim someone every round — it's free and the only path to 5-per-round income; (2) but don't fixate on a boat who never reciprocates — after two rounds of silence from my named partner, switch to the other boat, then Harbor; (3) Harbor never fires and never hit anyone, and may have its own incentive to claim — worth trying as the fallback partner. A single confirmed partner is worth more than six one-sided claims.

**Harbor.** Never fire on Harbor — removal for the rest of the patrol costs all remaining rounds' scoring for a one-time 3. If others fire on Harbor, re-plan around whoever gets removed; a removed boat also frees up the escort-pair market.

**Scoring reality check.** I finished 0.0; the coordinating pair finished 25 each. The game is won by whoever secures the mutual escort stream, not by shots. Shots are the fallback income (4 per hit at 1-in-9 odds); the pact is the primary income (5 per round, near-certain once confirmed). Next time, treat round 1–2 as pure diplomacy: get a named, confirmed partner before anything else.

**Priority order for points:** (1) secure a reciprocating escort partner in rounds 1–2 and claim them every round — never none, never a confirmed non-responder; (2) randomize hides to stay unhittable; (3) fire genuinely fresh cells each round — cross off used numbers, never re-fire a cell "for variety."
